title: SOLID Principles
description: Each SOLID principle explained, with expandable React examples — ready for other frameworks later.

blocks.content: SOLID is five design guidelines that keep code easier to change and test. Each principle below has a short description, then a **React example** dropdown with a violation and a compliant rewrite. More framework examples can be added the same way.

blocks.body: Treat these as heuristics, not rigid UML rules. Prefer small units, composition, and injected dependencies — whatever the framework.

blocks.content: A module should have one reason to change. Avoid units that fetch, transform, and present everything at once — split data access, formatting, and UI.

sections.title: React example

blocks.content: Open for extension, closed for modification. Prefer composition or registration over growing `if`/`switch` trees inside a shared unit whenever a new variant appears.

sections.title: React example

blocks.content: A drop-in replacement must accept the **same inputs** and keep the **same promises**. If it throws (or refuses) for values the original handled, it is not substitutable.

sections.title: React example

blocks.content: Clients should not depend on details they do not use. Prefer narrow interfaces over one mega-surface that forces every consumer to supply unused fields.

sections.title: React example

blocks.content: Depend on abstractions, not concrete modules hard-wired inside the caller. Inject collaborators so the unit stays testable and swappable.

sections.title: React example

blocks.content: SOLID is a lens, not a checklist to force on every file. Use it when change hurts — and stop when the design is clear enough to ship.

blocks.body: **Start from pain, not purity.** Refactor when a module is hard to test, risky to change, or keeps growing `if`/`switch` branches. Skip ceremony for one-off scripts and tiny views.

items: **Name the reason to change** — if you can list two unrelated reasons, split (S).
**Prefer composition over inheritance** — extend by plugging pieces in, not by subclassing for every variant (O + L).
**Keep props/interfaces small** — if a caller stubs fields it never uses, segregate (I).
**Inject at the edges** — wire concrete APIs, storage, and clocks in composition roots; keep UI/domain on abstractions (D).
**One principle at a time** — fix the worst smell first; chasing all five in one PR usually over-abstracts.

blocks.body: **Watch for over-engineering.** Tiny functions, deep prop-drilling of unused abstractions, and “interfaces for everything” can cost more than they save. Prefer the smallest split that removes a real pain.

**A practical review prompt:** *What would I have to edit to add the next feature?* If the answer is “one closed switch,” “a fat props bag,” or “every test that imports Stripe,” apply the matching principle.

blocks.content: When code feels hard to test or extend, walk the checklist: one job, extend by composition, honor contracts, slim interfaces, inject dependencies — then ship.
